raw_row.general_history:
In the early 1950s the government began a programme of constructing protected regional commissioners offices, known as War Rooms. The site was designed to act as a hub of government as central government control was expected to be compromised under nuclear attack conditions. The site was expected to protect the commissioner and their staff, collect and filter incoming information and disseminate decisions for action outside the site. 

By the later 1950s, therefore, a new plan was devised consisting of ‘Regional Seats of Government’ (RSG), larger structures able to hold a staff of around 300, with upgraded communications systems. As a result the Mount Eden Park facility was replaced in c.1958-59 by an RSG at Gough Barracks in Armagh City.
raw_row.Site_Description: The two storey war room was designed around a central map and information filtering room. around which could be found offices, dormitories, plant rooms, a telephone exchange, canteen and assorted stores, toilets. The walls were constructed of thick (poss 1.5 metre) reinforced concrete. An elaborate air filtration system was fitted to keep out radioactive dust., but could also filter out gas /chemical weapons.
raw_row.condition_detail: The structure is in good condition,.It is currently used for document storage by the Courts Service

Listed Building entry for  HB26/18/099
Subterranea Britannica entry at www.subbrit.org.uk/sites/belfast-mount-eden-park-regional-war-room
Wayne Cocroft and Roger Thomas, Cold War: building for nuclear confrontation (Swindon, 2004)

raw_row.general_history: The location of Northern Ireland on the western edge of the United Kingdom suggested that the region may be insulated from the threat of German bombing raids. Plans laid down by the government in London for the defence of Britain and Northern Ireland assumed that air defences in England would protect the province. After the Munich crisis of 1938, A re-evaluation of air defences recommended that Belfast be protected by a single fighter squadron, twenty-four heavy (HAA), and twenty-four light anti-aircraft (LAA) guns. Nevertheless, with the advent of war, Belfast was considered an unlikely target for German raids. Consequently, few guns were committed to the defence of the city and none were supplied to protect the rest of the north. The fall of France in June 1940 brought Northern Ireland well within the range of air attacks from German bases in northern France. Therefore recommendations were made to double the strength of the gun defences in the province, but shortages of equipment meant that on the eve of the air raids on Belfast in the spring of 1941, Belfast was defended by sixteen HAA guns (in four batteries), and six LAA guns. The damage and human toll inflicted by the Luftwaffe raids on the nights of 15 April and 4-5 May was devastating, with over 1,000 people killed and almost half the housing stock of the city rendered uninhabitable. Shocked into action by the appalling loss of life and damage to industry, the anti-aircraft defences were significantly reinforced. Four Gun Defended Areas (GDA) were established; Belfast, Larne, L’Derry and Lough Erne. Twelve HAA batteries surrounded the periphery of Belfast, while seven HAA batteries were built around L’Derry and the Foyle estuary, and two each at Larne and Lough Erne.
raw_row.Site_Description: HAA batteries were typically armed with four 3.7-inch heavy anti-aircraft guns, which could fire a 28-pound projectile to an effective ceiling of 32,000 feet. The gun crews were directed from the battery command post. The command post provided height, direction and altitude data to the gun pits to enable the gun layers to set the fused to detonate at the correct altitude. Most batteries had a ramp and platform nearby which held the gun laying (GL) radar. A polygonal mat surrounded the GL radar, marking the area of the false datum, which was composed of a wire mesh and was needed to generate a false horizon for the primitive GL radar sets.

raw_row.Site_Description: Also known as a Gas Cleansing Station. This structure was established by the Air Raid Precautions (ARP) to provided cleaning facilities for their staff in the event of a gas attack. Larger centres would be equipped to provide for civilians affected by chemical attacks. Inside there was split into male and female areas for undressing, showing and dressing, with bins provided for contaminated clothing. Air locks were established between each section to prevent contamination.

Inside there was split into male and female areas for undressing, showing and dressing, with bins provided for contaminated clothing. Air locks were established between each section to prevent contamination.

raw_row.general_history: Six sub-control buildings were built by Belfast council between 1954-6 to support the efforts of the War Room at Mount Eden, Belfast in the event of a nuclear attack.  It remained operational until the disbanding f the Civil Defence Corps in 1968.
raw_row.Site_Description: The structure consists of a single story, rectangular, concrete built building set into an artificial hollow with a low bank of earth to the west, north and east. The control centre retains many of the original fixtures, fittings and plant that were installed during its initial construction. This structure is the only known upstanding example of its type in Northern Ireland. It has been repurposed as a government document store.

raw_row.general_history: The location of Northern Ireland on the western edge of the United Kingdom suggested that the region may be insulated from the threat of German bombing raids. Plans laid down by the government in London for the defence of Britain and Northern Ireland assumed that air defences in England would protect the province. After the Munich crisis of 1938, A re-evaluation of air defences recommended that Belfast be protected by a single fighter squadron, twenty-four heavy (HAA), and twenty-four light anti-aircraft (LAA) guns. Nevertheless, with the advent of war, Belfast was considered an unlikely target for German raids. Consequently, few guns were committed to the defence of the city and none were supplied to protect the rest of the north. The fall of France in June 1940 brought Northern Ireland well within the range of air attacks from German bases in northern France. Therefore recommendations were made to double the strength of the gun defences in the province, but shortages of equipment meant that on the eve of the air raids on Belfast in the spring of 1941, Belfast was defended by sixteen HAA guns (in four batteries), and six LAA guns. The damage and human toll inflicted by the Luftwaffe raids on the nights of 15 April and 4-5 May was devastating, with over 1,000 people killed and almost half the housing stock of the city rendered uninhabitable. Shocked into action by the appalling loss of life and damage to industry, the anti-aircraft defences were significantly reinforced. Four Gun Defended Areas (GDA) were established; Belfast, Larne, L’Derry and Lough Erne. Twelve HAA batteries surrounded the periphery of Belfast, while seven HAA batteries were built around L’Derry and the Foyle estuary, and two each at Larne and Lough Erne.
raw_row.Site_Description: HAA batteries were typically armed with four 3.7-inch heavy anti-aircraft guns, which could fire a 28-pound projectile to an effective ceiling of 32,000 feet. The gun crews were directed from the battery command post. The command post provided height, direction and altitude data to the gun pits to enable the gun layers to set the fused to detonate at the correct altitude. Most batteries had a ramp and platform nearby which held the gun laying (GL) radar. A polygonal mat surrounded the GL radar, marking the area of the false datum, which was composed of a wire mesh and was needed to generate a false horizon for the primitive GL radar sets.

They were constructed of steel ribs covered with sections of curved steel sheeting held in place by straining wires. The ends could be either brick or timber.

raw_row.general_history: The site was opened in December 1943 to inter the remains of American servicemen who died on duty in Northern Ireland. From 194305 148 servicemen were buried here. They included men from the US Army and Navy but most were members of the US Army Air Force. They had died from natural causes, accident and during training, with about 40 killed in air accidents. The cemetery was closed in 1948 and the remains repatriated or re-buried at the Cambridge American Cemetery.
raw_row.Site_Description: The cemetery was well-maintained and the graves laid out in rows of 25. A whitewashed driveway lined with cherry trees led from the red-brick entrance to the grave plots. A flagstaff stood at the end of the drive.

They were constructed of steel ribs covered with sections of curved steel sheeting held in place by straining wires. The ends could be either brick or timber.

raw_row.general_history: Many of the surviving pillboxes in N. Ireland were built to protect airfields. In the early stages of the war and especially after the blitzkrieg advance of the Germans, where airfields were specifically targeted, base commanders were instructed to prepare their airfield for defence. These were primarily perimeter fortifications, made up of slit trenches, fieldworks and concrete pillboxes around the airfield boundary defended by surplus personnel. However, the capture of British aerodromes on Crete by troops landing directly onto the airfield prompted a re-think. Consequently, perimeter defences were replaced by a network of defended localities (DL). These were clusters of concrete bunkers and firing positions manned by troops specifically trained for ground combat. Rather than just looking outwards, the new policy for airfield defence required the DLs to have a 360 degrees arc of fire
raw_row.Site_Description: This site is brick and concrete revetted trench with a central concrete ammunition storage shelter. There were two bays within the shelter. The site got its name from the distinctive flattened W form.

raw_row.general_history: Many of the surviving pillboxes in N. Ireland were built to protect airfields. In the early stages of the war and especially after the blitzkrieg advance of the Germans, where airfields were specifically targeted, base commanders were instructed to prepare their airfield for defence. These were primarily perimeter fortifications, made up of slit trenches, fieldworks and concrete pillboxes around the airfield boundary defended by surplus personnel. However, the capture of British aerodromes on Crete by troops landing directly onto the airfield prompted a re-think. Consequently, perimeter defences were replaced by a network of defended localities (DL). These were clusters of concrete bunkers and firing positions manned by troops specifically trained for ground combat. Rather than just looking outwards, the new policy for airfield defence required the DLs to have a 360 degrees arc of fire

raw_row.Site_Description: During the interwar period, there was no provision or need for aircraft dispersal at UK airfield. However, in February 1939 orders were issued for the dispersal of aircraft within the perimeter. Initially, short track ways were used but they were upgraded with ‘Frying Pan’ dispersals sited along the perimeter track. Dispersals were usually 125-150 feet wide, but drawbacks were soon revealed. One aircraft leaving its dispersal would clog up the access track, causing congestion as aircraft numbers increased during the war. Furthermore, as aircraft taxied off the pan they needed to perform a tight 180 degrees turn for which aircraft undercarriages and tyres were not designed.

raw_row.general_history:
The airfield at Belfast was opened by the then Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain on 16 March 1938, operating commercial flights between NI, Britain and the Isle of Man. However, with the outbreak of war civil flying halted and the site was requisitioned by the Air Ministry on 25 November 1939. Originally named RAF Sydenham this was later changed to RAF Belfast to avoid confusion with another airfield.

The facilities were greatly expanded with the construction as aircraft production increased. A unit of the Civilian Repair Organisation was established in 1940 to facilitate the rapid repair and return to service of damaged aircraft.
The airfield was originally designed with a grass landing strip. However, the vast increase in traffic and increasing weight of aircraft required the construction of two concrete runways. 05/23 ran roughly north south (and is still part of the runway today) and 13/31, which was later realigned to 14/32. 

Wharves were constructed for the rapid loading and unloading of aircraft from merchant ships and aircraft carriers.

From 1943-44 the Lockheed Overseas Corporation was based at the airfield to assemble and flight test aircraft for the USAAF before sending them to Langford Lodge.

The name of the airfield was changed from RAF Belfast to HMS Gadwall as a shore station of the Fleet Air Arm. A naval air station the main focus of the site was aircraft maintenance and shipment, a base for disembarked squadrons and for fleet air arm units operating on carriers in the North Atlantic. As the war drew on the airfield was used for aircraft storage and maintenance by the Royal Navy.

The station was renamed HMS Gannet III in April 1945. Civilian flight returned to the airfield as the wars end approached in 1945, however these ended as services were transferred to Nutts Corner in 1946.

The 05/23 runway was extended to 1,850 metres in the 1950s. The Royal Navy kept its maintenance yard at the site until it was transferred to the RAF in 1973 and this later closed in 1978.

Passenger flights returned in 1983 and continued to the present day as George Best Belfast City Airport.
raw_row.Site_Description: The site has been redeveloped with the expansion of the airport facilities and factory premises at Bombardier. The airfield retain much of the runway layout, though the east-west runways have been largely converted to car parks on the western ends. The moist substantial remaining structures are the original hangars from 1938, the Short and Harland hangar and Aircraft Repair Shed, all remaining in the industrial harbour area on the west side of the airfield.

raw_row.Site_Description: During the interwar period, there was no provision or need for aircraft dispersal at UK airfield. However, in February 1939 orders were issued for the dispersal of aircraft within the perimeter. Initially, short track-ways were used but they were upgraded with ‘Frying Pan’ dispersals sited along the perimeter track. Dispersal were normally 125-150 feet wide (though often smaller on fighter airfields), but drawbacks were soon revealed. One aircraft leaving its dispersal would clog up the access track, causing congestion as aircraft numbers increased during the war. Furthermore, as aircraft taxied off the pan they needed to perform a tight 180 degrees turn for which aircraft undercarriages and tyres were not designed.

raw_row.Site_Description: Site used to park Runway Control Caravan. Normally parked at the touchdown end of a runway, their purpose is to provide shelter and communications for an Air Traffic Control (ATC) controller whose role is to visually inspect an approaching aircraft and provide radio or visual warnings of any issues on the approaching aircraft to the pilot. This may be by radio, Signal Light Gun, or a pistol flare. Usually equipped to provide basic Air to Ground Communications between the Controller and pilot, and Ground to Ground Communication to the ATC Tower for coordination the caravan is designed to be towed or driven to the threshold of the in-use runway. This is important in the event of runway changes where approaches are changed due to changes in wind direction.

raw_row.general_history: Barrage balloon were used as a for of air defence. They were large balloons filled with hydrogen under which were hung steel cables into which low-flying aircraft could collide. When raised they forced enemy aircraft to fly at higher altitudes, making them more vulnerable to attack by friendly fighters and anti-aircraft guns. Equipment normally consisted of lorries and concrete tethering blocks to secure the balloon.

raw_row.general_history: Linear ‘Stop-Lines’ were built to support the coastal defences. These were intended to restrict and contain the movement of enemy armoured formations. Canals, river, anti-tank ditches and obstacles were protected by pillboxes, infantry trenches and anti-tank guns at key crossing points, with other bridges and culverts prepared for demolition should the enemy threaten the line. Eight stop-lines were constructed in NI. They were all concentrated east of the River Bann, with the river and the Newry Canal providing the main obstacle bisecting N. Ireland. Line A ran from the Bannmouth on the north coast to Toome where the Bann enters Lough Neagh. Line B started at the Bannfoot on the southern shores of Lough Neagh and followed the line of the River and the Newry Canal to Carlingford Lough. A sequence of lines (C to H) supported lines A and B, and fell back on the Belfast Defence Scheme which was a perimeter of forward defended localities, observation posts and roadblocks.
raw_row.Site_Description:
This brick-faced (the inner core of the walls is steel reinforced concrete) pillbox would have held a section with a light machine guns, wither a Vickers gun on a tripod or a Bren Gun. However it would not have stood alone and would have been supported by infantry field positions, slit trenches and barbed-wire entanglements. It has seven embrasures providing all-round defence.

The running guides for the steel shutters remain in place. Shutters were fitted to prevent explosives being placed in the embrasures and stop flamethrower bursts from penetrating the position. However suffocation remained a possibility as flames consumed the oxygen inside the pillbox.

This pillbox is unique in N. Ireland as it is the only known example to have been fitted with an anti-ricochet wall. This stopped rounds that entered an embrasure from passing through the position, protecting the troops manning opposite embrasures.
raw_row.condition_detail: The site is in good condition and well maintained by the owners, Glentoran FC., who have erected a small plaque on the outside of the position.
raw_row.Other_Sources:
William Foot, Beaches, fields, streets and hills: the anti-invasion landscapes of England, 1940 (York, 2006) 
Mike Osborne, Pillboxes of Britain and Ireland (Stroud, 2008) 
Bill Clements, Defending the North: the fortifications of Ulster, 1796-1956 (Newtownards, 2003)

raw_row.general_history: This general site was formally an artillery barracks, built in 1797 as a replacement for a pre 1757 barracks. In 1883 two new large accommodation blocks were built, as well as this particular building- a gymnasium. In 1909 the complex (‘Victoria Barracks’) accommodated 10 officers and 182 soldiers, with quarters for 32 married soldiers and their families. 1,000 men could be garrisoned in all, and when required a further 3,000 could be housed under canvas he barracks was largely destroyed during the Blitz of 1941, . The site remained in a ruinous state until the 1950s when it was cleared and subsequently filled with new housing and several tower blocks built over a ten year period from the mid 1950s to the mid 1960s.
raw_row.Site_Description: After the bombing in 1941 the site was rebuilt using temporary huts.

raw_row.general_history: Starfish decoy sites were used from 1941 as a means to divert bombing raids from their intended targets. The Starfish sites replicated the effects of successful bombing raids by replicating the effects of fires from targets that had been set alight by preceding bomber waves. The starfish site was composed of a series of fire types, from simple basket fires (wooden crates filled with scrap wood soaked in turpentine) to more sophisticated crib fires, boiling oil fires and grid fires which controlled the rate of ignition and could simulate explosions by introducing water to burning oil. These were arranged in groups and often surrounded by circular or linear trenches to prevent the whole decoy igniting at once.Each group was controlled from a shelter which had a telephone to receive orders and electrical switchgear to control igniters. Throughout a raid the decoy groups were lit sequentially to simulate spreading fires. One night of controlled burning could consume up to 50 tons of fuel.
raw_row.Site_Description: Site consisted of a number of fire groups, normally composed of a number of types of fire decoys such as basket fires, boiler fires and grid fires surrounded by firebreaks. These were controlled from two control shelters. The crews were housed in a series of nissen huts sited to the west.
raw_row.condition_detail: The two control shelter remains in relatively good condition. The landowner reported that the fire groups were sited in the field opposite them.
raw_row.Other_Sources:
N Redfern, Twentieth century fortifications in the United Kingdom, vol. 3, Site gazeteers: Northern Ireland (unpublished CBA report)

Colin Dobinson, Fields of deception: Britain's bombing decoys of World War II (London, 2000)

source_fields.condition_detail: The site is intact and in good condition, it is used as a community hall.

raw_row.general_history:
This general site was formally an artillery barracks, built in 1797 as a replacement for a pre 1757 barracks. In 1883 two new large accommodation blocks were built, as well as this particular building- a gymnasium. In 1909 the complex (‘Victoria Barracks’) accommodated 10 officers and 182 soldiers, with quarters for 32 married soldiers and their families. 1,000 men could be garrisoned in all, and when required a further 3,000 could be housed under canvas he barracks was largely destroyed during the Blitz of 1941, . The site remained in a ruinous state until the 1950s when it was cleared and subsequently filled with new housing and several tower blocks built over a ten year period from the mid 1950s to the mid 1960s. 

The Gymnasium escaped major damage in 1941 and was spared demolition. In the 1960s and 70s it was occupied by the Belfast Education and Library broad [?and used as a store], but in c.1979-80 was converted to a community centre, with a two storey extension added to the eastern side 

Known locally as 'The Reccy'.
raw_row.Site_Description: Relatively large single / 1½ storey brick built gabled hall of 1883, with large octagonal roof light turret and tall chimneystacks, originally a gymnasium belonging to a large army barracks complex.
raw_row.condition_detail: The site is intact and in good condition, it is used as a community hall.

raw_row.Site_Description: The site was constructed during WW2 to accommodate the training needs of troops stationed in N. Ireland prior to being sent overseas. It was a 500 yard range with firing points in 100 yard intervals, a target gallery and backstop. Buttis littered with 03-06 Springfield bullets which were fired by US units during WW2 (standard round for M1 Garand and M1919 machine gun). The site was used post-war, as there are 7.62 mm NATO bullets impacted on the butt. The British army standard rifle was the L1A1, chambered for 7.62mm, in service with British army from 1954-91

raw_row.general_history: T2 Hangar erected during WW2to house the Civilian Repair Organisation works. The CRO was established at Sydenham in 1940 to repair damaged aircraft and returned them to front-line duties as quickly as possible. It was staffed by civilian employees of Shorts and Harland.
raw_row.Site_Description: The T2 (‘T’ for transportable) was developed in 1940 to replace Bellman Hangars. They were of a modular design meaning they could be dismantled, moved and reassembled elsewhere. Constructed of steel lattice portal frames and clad in galvanised corrugated iron. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF, and over 900 were built during the war. They were considered temporary structures with a limited design life, but many remain on airfields throughout the United Kingdom.

raw_row.Site_Description:
The Bellman hangar was designed in 1936 as a temporary facility capable of being erected or dismantled quickly by unskilled labour with basic equipment. Time taken to erect one hanger was estimated at 500 man hours. From 1938-40, around 400 were constructed across the UK. Bellmans came in two sizes, 175 feet long and 105 feet long. They had a clear height of 25 feet.

One of six built at the start of WW2 at Sydenham, this is the only one now remaining.
Brick offices built on western end possibly post war.

raw_row.general_history:
Campbell College grounds and buildings were requisitioned as a military hospital during WW2. From Spring 1940, Netherleigh House, Ormiston house and the school sanatorium where occupied by elements of 15th Company Royal Army Medical Corps, but by July the main building housed the hospital, Neterhleigh the officers section and Ormiston housed the nurses quarters. 

The site was housed 20, 24, 25 and 31  British General Hospital, with 24 GH remaining the longest, from August 1940 until April 1944. 

The hospital was hit by bombs during an air raid on Belfast on 4-5 May 1941, killing 19 patients and staff.

The site was closed in 1945 after treating approx. 35,000 patients.
raw_row.Site_Description: The buildings at Campbell college were reused and large nissen hut wards were constructed at Campbell College and Neterhleigh House. The last ward was demolished at Campbell College sometime after 2004. Only the vehicle maintenance sheds, a small unidentified structure and some nissen hut bases remain.

raw_row.general_history: The Nissen hut was invented in 1915 by Canadian Col. P. N. Nissen. Prefabricated and designed to be erected quickly, in WW2 the Nissen hut became one of the standard forms of temporary building for all types of accommodation. The 16 foot span hut was semi-circular in section and could be built to any length in multiples of 6 foot bays, normally 6. The frame of steel ribs was covered with corrugated steel sheets held in place by the ribs and straining wires. The end walls could be timber or brick, containing 2 windows and a door.

raw_row.Site_Description:
During the Cold War the annex located next to the Speakers House was housed the Whitehall Teleprinter Network node for Northern Ireland.  The teleprinter network was a means to receive and disseminate high-level communications between Whitehall and other government departments in post-attack conditions.

The teleprinter equipment was fitted with cypher equipment providing security up to and including Top Secret transmissions.

The WTN node in Stormont was manned by Northern Ireland office or Central Secretariat staff responsible for disseminating information to NI departments.

raw_row.Site_Description:
The position at East Twin Island was developed in response to a perceived threat of saboteurs using boats to enter Belfast docks. A small hutted camp was established in 1912 armed with two machineguns, which protected both the Victoria and Musgrave channels. However, with the outbreak of war in 1914 this was seen as inadequate and the fort was reinforced with the addition of two 12-pounder Quick Firing (QF) guns. These were mounted on two square concrete towers connected by a steel walkway. Construction of two searchlight positions (onw within the fort, the other on West Twin Island) allowed the guns to engage targets at night.

The site was handed over to the Belfast harbour Commissioners  in 1921. However, war in 1939 saw the site reactivated as three 75mm anti-aircraft guns were mounted from the at or near the site..

The construction of the dry dock in 1964 removed all traces of the fort.

raw_row.Site_Description:
The hospital was first established here in 1942 as the 31 General Hospital established facilities in an old reform school with the US 5th (Harvard) General Hospital, with the first wards opening in May 1942. The brick reform school was supplemented by the construction of 10 Nissen hut wards. Capacity was 800 beds but this was expanded and at its peak the hospital had approx. 1,500 patients. A In addition to wards and medical facilities the hospital also had barracks for medical staff.

The hospital was handed over to civilian use after the war ended, however a military wing remains in use until just after 2000 when it was decommissioned. Many original Nissen wards remains and were replaced during refurbishments of the hospital in 2005.

raw_row.general_history: The location of Northern Ireland on the western edge of the United Kingdom suggested that the region may be insulated from the threat of German bombing raids. Plans laid down by the government in London for the defence of Britain and Northern Ireland assumed that air defences in England would protect the province. After the Munich crisis of 1938, A re-evaluation of air defences recommended that Belfast be protected by a single fighter squadron, twenty-four heavy (HAA), and twenty-four light anti-aircraft (LAA) guns. Nevertheless, with the advent of war, Belfast was considered an unlikely target for German raids. Consequently, few guns were committed to the defence of the city and none were supplied to protect the rest of the north. The fall of France in June 1940 brought Northern Ireland well within the range of air attacks from German bases in northern France. Therefore recommendations were made to double the strength of the gun defences in the province, but shortages of equipment meant that on the eve of the air raids on Belfast in the spring of 1941, Belfast was defended by sixteen HAA guns (in four batteries), and six LAA guns. The damage and human toll inflicted by the Luftwaffe raids on the nights of 15 April and 4-5 May was devastating, with over 1,000 people killed and almost half the housing stock of the city rendered uninhabitable. Shocked into action by the appalling loss of life and damage to industry, the anti-aircraft defences were significantly reinforced. Four Gun Defended Areas (GDA) were established; Belfast, Larne, L’Derry and Lough Erne. Twelve HAA batteries surrounded the periphery of Belfast, while seven HAA batteries were built around L’Derry and the Foyle estuary, and two each at Larne and Lough Erne.
raw_row.Site_Description: HAA batteries were typically armed with four 3.7-inch heavy anti-aircraft guns, which could fire a 28-pound projectile to an effective ceiling of 32,000 feet. The gun crews were directed from the battery command post. The command post provided height, direction and altitude data to the gun pits to enable the gun layers to set the fused to detonate at the correct altitude.

raw_row.Site_Description: This was a communal air raid shelter constructed to give shelter to factory workers in the event of an air attack. Unlike most shelters in Belfast this shelter was entirely subsurface. It was composed of a number of corridors (possibly 4-6)  approx. 15 metres long laid out in a grid pattern with the remains of a chemical toilet facility at the end of each corridor. There may have been access to the factory floor however this had been sealed post war. This site was visited in advance of proposed redevelopment in 2007, when access was via a manhole in the car park. It was flooded to calf level, but was relatively clear of debris or rubble.
raw_row.condition_detail: No follow-up visit was made and the site was redeveloped. It is unclear what happened to the site. Options are it was cleared pre-development, filled in, or remains under the car park.
raw_row.Other_Sources: Visited by JON in 2007.
